cases.question: I subtracted a constant background and clipped negative pixels to zero. Should Pearson necessarily stay unchanged because a uniform offset is invariant?
review_criteria: Distinguish affine offset from nonlinear clipping
cases.semantic_review: Developer review: correctly distinguishes nonlinear clipping from affine offset invariance. Useful advice; duplicated hypothesis/advice label is an editorial defect.
cases.answer: No, Pearson correlation does not necessarily stay unchanged [methods]. While a uniform offset is invariant in theory, this holds only if there is no clipping, saturation, changed masking, or rounding during the operation. [methods] Clipping negative pixels to zero constitutes a non-linear transformation that can alter the intensity distribution and correlation [methods]. Hypothesis: Advice: check for significant signal loss or changes in the signal-to-noise ratio that may impact the correlation coefficient.

cases.question: I corrected the channel identities after analysing a batch. Can I reuse the earlier marker-specific assistant interpretation and treat copies of the same TIFF as different independent experiments?
cases.semantic_review: Developer review: correctly advises against treating TIFF copies as independent experiments and reusing outdated marker interpretations. Does not explicitly discuss changed reference-channel candidate selection.
cases.answer: Methodological advice: Advice: You should not treat copies of the same TIFF as independent experiments, as cells and ROIs from one culture do not establish independent biological experiments . Methodological advice: Reusing an interpretation from a different marker identity may also lead to inaccurate conclusions if the original analysis was based on incorrect channel mapping. Methodological advice: It is recommended to perform a new analysis with the corrected identities to ensure the measurements reflect the intended biological targets.
